A bathroom refresh: decide what stays before pricing what changes

A practical scope checklist for Halton homeowners, including where local permits and electrical requirements enter the conversation.

Arin home notes · Published October 22, 2026

If your bathroom feels tired, start by naming the problem instead of choosing a demolition date. Is the issue worn paint, awkward storage, a damaged finish, or a layout that no longer works? A new mirror and refreshed cabinetry answer a different brief from moving a shower. Mixing the two makes an estimate difficult to interpret.

Draw two lists: stays and changes

On a simple room sketch, mark the toilet, basin, bath or shower, doorway, and existing lights. Then make a “stays” list and a “changes” list. Be explicit about fixtures that will remain in their current position and about any wall, plumbing, or electrical changes you are considering.

In Oakville, the town’s interior-alteration guidance distinguishes decorative work from changes such as wall removal and adding or relocating plumbing fixtures. It says permits typically are not required for replacing existing cabinetry, sinks, faucets, toilets, and cosmetic surface changes. Note the word “typically”: it doesn’t clear every bathroom project. [1]

Check the property and the municipality

Use the written scope when contacting your municipal building team. Ask which approvals and documents apply to that property and that work before committing to a start date. For Milton projects, start with the town’s building-permit hub rather than assuming an Oakville example settles a Milton application. [3]

Have the address, an existing-versus-proposed sketch, and any condominium or other property-management requirements available. If the scope changes after that conversation, ask whether the approval requirements change too. Keep the response with the project notes so everyone is working from the same understanding.

Keep electrical responsibilities visible

A general renovation scope should identify who will carry out any electrical work. The Electrical Safety Authority states that when a general contractor subcontracts electrical work, it must be done by a Licensed Electrical Contractor. Ask for the contracting business’s ECRA/ESA licence details and verify them with ESA. [2]

Also ask the electrical contractor which notification and inspection steps apply and who is arranging them. ESA’s guidance describes notification and inspection as part of the electrical work process; these questions should be settled before work is concealed, not at the decorating stage. [4]

Write a brief someone can actually estimate

  • Keep: fixtures, walls, and finishes that stay, with their locations.
  • Change: each replacement or alteration, including who supplies it.
  • Known issues: leaks, loose finishes, previous repairs, or access problems.
  • Daily use: whether another bathroom is available during the work.
  • Approvals: who confirms requirements and obtains relevant permissions.
  • Unknowns: how findings after opening a surface will be documented and approved.

Bring that same brief to each discussion. Two proposals can then be compared against an agreed scope rather than the vague label “bathroom renovation.” Choose the finishes once you understand which work they depend on.
